title: The China-United States rivalry
subtitle: 21st century
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Two political models, two technological ambitions, one planet. Why the rivalry between **Beijing** and **Washington** shapes the whole century.

hero.hook: In forty years, a country poorer than its neighbors became the only credible rival of the United States.

blocks.text: The rivalry between **China** and the **United States** has become the most important relationship of the 21st century. It is not only an economic race: it sets two political models, two technological ambitions and two visions of world order against each other.

After the **Cold War**, the United States seemed to have no serious rival. China's lightning rise changed that. Some researchers now speak of the **[[Thucydides Trap]]**: the situation, seen several times in history, in which a rising power threatens to overtake an established one, and confrontation becomes almost impossible to avoid.

sections.title: From isolation to the factory of the world

blocks.text: In 1978, China came out of decades of internal turmoil exhausted. Under **Deng Xiaoping**, the country changed course and launched the “Four Modernizations,” breaking with communist orthodoxy to adopt a form of capitalism supervised by the Party.

The strategy rested on opening up to foreign capital. Special economic zones, with **Shenzhen** as their symbol, drew in companies with tax breaks and cheap labor. That is how China became “the factory of the world.”
China is the biggest creditor of the United States: it holds about 800 billion dollars of American debt. A sudden break would therefore ruin both economies at once.
Its entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001 opened an expansion without precedent. In 2010 it passed Japan and became the second largest economy in the world.

The shift from cooperation to open rivalry took shape under the presidencies of **Donald Trump** and **Xi Jinping**. Washington accused Beijing of unfair trade practices and technology theft, and imposed heavy tariffs on Chinese goods.

The real heart of the conflict moved to high technology. The Americans have tried to cut China off from **semiconductors**, the chips that artificial intelligence and modern weapons cannot do without. This is what is called [[Technological "decoupling"]].
Companies such as Huawei and TikTok are seen in Washington as threats to national security. The policy continued after Trump left office, proof that the rivalry cuts across American party lines.

In military terms, the confrontation shifts toward Southeast Asia. Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a zone essential to world trade and rich in resources. To assert its sovereignty, China has turned reefs into artificial islands with military bases.

blocks.caption: Taiwan and the South China Sea have become the main point of military friction between Beijing and Washington

blocks.text: The most sensitive point remains **Taiwan**. Beijing treats the island as a rebel province to be reunified. Taiwan, however, receives growing support from the United States. A conflict in the strait would paralyze world shipping and the supply of computer chips, since the island makes the most advanced ones.

Feeling encircled, Xi Jinping has rolled out the “New Silk Roads,” an investment program in more than 140 countries that lets China secure its supplies and build a network of influence to set against the West.

Beyond the numbers, this rivalry is also ideological. It sets the Western liberal model, built on democracy and human rights, against the Chinese model of fast economic growth directed by a single party.

For many developing countries, Chinese efficiency offers an attractive alternative to Western aid, which often comes with democratic conditions attached. China is no longer content to join the international system: it now wants to reform it so that it reflects Chinese power more closely.

The relationship is entering a phase of systemic competition. For now the two countries avoid open war, but a new technological **[[Cold War]]** looks hard to avoid, and it is forcing the rest of the world to choose between the two blocs of power.

In 1978, China was poorer than many developing countries. Forty years of record growth later, it is the only power able to challenge the United States on every front: economic, military and technological.
